**The Case for Lingering**

I have been thinking lately about the way a day felt longer when I was a child. Not because time moved differently, but because I had not yet learned to fill every silence with a task. There were empty afternoons that stretched like taffy, hours with no purpose except to watch dust drift through sunlight or listen to the refrigerator hum. Those moments were not wasted. They were the raw material of a private world.

Somewhere along the way, I began to treat time as a resource to be optimized. I reach for my phone between brushing my teeth and making coffee. I listen to podcasts at double speed while folding laundry. I feel a small thrill at clearing my inbox to zero, as if deleting words were an achievement. This is the ambient condition of modern life: a low-grade fever of productivity that tells us every moment must be accounted for, improved, or converted into output.

But I want to make a case for lingering. Not laziness, but a deliberate refusal to hurry through the parts of life that have no measurable outcome. Lingering is staying with something a little longer than necessary: letting the tea cool, watching the neighbor’s cat stretch on the fence, rereading a paragraph because it sounds beautiful, not because it contains information. Lingering is inefficient. It produces nothing. And yet it is in these unproductive stretches that I often feel most like myself.

The pressure to optimize comes from many directions: economic fear, and the glowing rectangles in our pockets. The smartphone is the greatest enemy of lingering ever invented. It fills every gap with content. Waiting for a bus? Scroll. Standing in line? Scroll. The algorithm captures loose attention that might otherwise drift toward the sky or the faces of strangers. It converts idleness into engagement, and engagement into data. We are never bored, and so we are never truly alone with our thoughts.

Boredom is not a problem to be solved. It is a threshold. Many of my best ideas have arrived not when I was trying to think but when I was doing something mindless: washing dishes, walking, staring out a train window. Rebecca Solnit described walking as a way to “lose oneself in order to find oneself,” and the same is true of any slow, undirected activity. When we stop demanding that our thoughts be useful, they wander into interesting territory.

There is a strange guilt attached to lingering. If I sit on a bench for twenty minutes without checking my phone, I feel I should be doing something. The guilt is not based on actual obligation; it is a vague sense that stillness is failure. Partly, it is learned. We are praised as children for being busy, not for watching clouds. But the ability to be still is a skill, and like any skill, it requires practice. It also requires permission—permission we rarely give ourselves.

The places where lingering is still permitted are transitional: airports, waiting rooms, the last hour before bed. No one expects productivity while waiting for a delayed flight, so you might read slowly or watch the departure board flicker. There is a texture to that time, thick and slightly melancholy, like light in a Hopper painting. I remember those in-between hours more vividly than many scheduled activities. They are not achievements, but experiences, and experiences are what we are made of.

Perhaps we avoid lingering because it brings us face to face with ourselves. When the phone is down, we have to sit with whatever is present. Sometimes that is uncomfortable; worries, regrets, and half-formed fears wait in the quiet. But there is also peace, if we stay long enough. The first few minutes are restless. Then something shifts. The internal chatter quiets, and the world becomes vivid: wind in the trees, the weight of the body, the slow drift of clouds. This is not escapism but a return to the texture of being alive.

I practice lingering deliberately. I walk without headphones. I leave my phone in another room while eating dinner. I sit on the front steps with coffee and watch the street. These practices feel small, but they have changed the quality of my days. I notice more. I feel less fragmented. I am less likely to reach the end of the evening and wonder where the time went, because I was there for it.

The resistance is strong. The pull of the phone is a tide. I still catch myself reaching for it, not from desire but habit. But habits can be redirected. Keep a comfortable chair by the window. Choose a walking route with no destination. Let the tea steep and do nothing while it steeps. These are not grand gestures. They are quiet acts of reclamation.

What would it mean to measure a day not by accomplishments but by what we noticed? To treat the quality of our attention as wealth? We might stop hurrying through meals, stop checking phones during conversations, stop treating rest as mere preparation for work. We might discover that the moments we had been rushing through were the point all along. The poem is not the punctuation at the end; it is the line breaks, the breath, the space between words.

Lingering is not a rejection of action. Action and stillness are partners. The farmer knows there is a time to plant and a time to let the field lie fallow. With fallow periods, the soil regains richness; without them, the field yields dust.

So I am giving myself permission to linger. I am learning to sit with the discomfort of an unfilled hour, practicing the art of staying a little longer, looking a little closer, breathing a little slower. The old guilt still rises, whispering about wasted time. But I suspect the only truly wasted time is the time we spend without noticing we are alive. The rest—the slow afternoons, the aimless walks, the quiet cups of tea—is the very substance of a life, waiting for us if we will only stop long enough to let it in.

Essay:

The Lost Art of Lingering

I have been thinking lately about the way a day used to feel longer when I was a child. Not because time moved differently in any physical sense, but because I had not yet learned to fill every silence with a task. There were empty afternoons that stretched like taffy, hours with no purpose except to watch dust drift through a shaft of sunlight or to lie on the floor and listen to the refrigerator hum. Those moments were not wasted. They were the raw material of a private world.

Somewhere along the way, I became a person who treats time as a resource to be optimized. I catch myself reaching for my phone in the brief interval between brushing my teeth and making coffee. I listen to podcasts at double speed while folding laundry. I have, on more than one occasion, felt a small thrill of satisfaction at clearing my inbox to zero, as if I had achieved something meaningful rather than simply deleted words. This is not a unique affliction. It is the ambient condition of modern life, a low-grade fever of productivity that tells us every moment must be accounted for, improved, or converted into output.

But I want to make a case for lingering. Not laziness, exactly, but a deliberate refusal to hurry through the parts of life that have no measurable outcome. Lingering is the act of staying with something a little longer than necessary: letting the tea cool, watching the neighbor’s cat stretch on the fence, rereading a paragraph because it sounds beautiful, not because it contains information. Lingering is inefficient. It produces nothing. And yet it is in these unproductive stretches that I often feel most like myself.

The pressure to optimize comes from many directions. There is the economic pressure, of course: the sense that if we are not working, we are falling behind. But there is also a subtler pressure, one that arrives through the glowing rectangles we carry in our pockets. The smartphone is the greatest enemy of lingering ever invented. It fills every gap with content. Waiting for a bus? Scroll. Standing in line? Scroll. Sitting on a park bench? Scroll. The algorithm is designed to capture whatever loose attention might otherwise drift toward the sky or the faces of strangers. It converts idleness into engagement, and engagement into data. We are never bored, and so we are never truly alone with our thoughts.

Boredom, though, is not a problem to be solved. It is a threshold. Many of my best ideas have arrived not when I was trying to think but when I was doing something mindless: washing dishes, walking a familiar route, staring out a train window. In those moments, the mind is free to make unexpected connections. The writer Rebecca Solnit once described walking as a way to “lose oneself in order to find oneself,” and I think the same is true of any slow, undirected activity. When we stop demanding that our thoughts be useful, they begin to wander into interesting territory.

There is a strange guilt attached to lingering. If I sit on a bench for twenty minutes without checking my phone, I feel like I should be doing something. The guilt is not based on any actual obligation; it is a vague, ambient sense that stillness is a form of failure. I wonder where that guilt comes from. Partly, it is learned. We are praised as children for being busy, for finishing our homework, for practicing the piano. We are not usually praised for watching clouds. But the ability to be still is a skill, and like any skill, it requires practice. It also requires permission—permission we rarely give ourselves.

The places where lingering is still permitted are often transitional: airports, waiting rooms, the last hour before bed. In these spaces, the usual rules are suspended. No one expects you to be productive while waiting for a delayed flight, so you might read a magazine slowly, or eat a sandwich without multitasking, or simply sit and watch the departure board flicker. There is a particular texture to that kind of time. It is thick and slightly melancholy, like the light in a Hopper painting. I find that I remember those in-between hours more vividly than many of my scheduled activities. They are not achievements, but they are experiences, and experiences are what we are actually made of.

Perhaps the reason we avoid lingering is that it brings us face to face with ourselves. When the phone is down and the to-do list is out of reach, we have to sit with whatever is actually present. Sometimes that is uncomfortable. There are worries, regrets, and half-formed fears waiting in the quiet. But there is also a kind of peace, if we can stay long enough to reach it. The first few minutes of stillness are often restless. Then something shifts. The internal chatter quiets, and the world outside becomes more vivid: the sound of wind in the trees, the weight of your own body on the chair, the slow drift of clouds. This is not escapism. It is the opposite—a return to the actual texture of being alive.

I have been trying to practice lingering deliberately. I take walks without headphones. I leave my phone in another room while I eat dinner. I sit on the front steps with a cup of coffee and do nothing but watch the street. These practices feel small, almost laughably simple, but they have changed the quality of my days. I notice more. I feel less fragmented. I am less likely to reach the end of the evening and wonder where the time went, because I was actually there for it.

The resistance to this practice is strong. The pull of the phone is like a tide. I still catch myself reaching for it, not because I want to see anything in particular, but because the habit has worn a groove in my brain. But habits can be redirected. The key, I think, is to make lingering easy and attractive. Keep a comfortable chair by the window. Choose a route for walking that has no destination. Let the tea steep for the full five minutes and do nothing while it steeps. These are not grand gestures. They are quiet acts of reclamation.

What would it mean to measure a day not by what we accomplished but by what we noticed? To count the quality of our attention as a form of wealth? I suspect it would change the way we live. We might stop hurrying through meals, stop checking our phones during conversations, stop treating rest as a mere preparation for more work. We might discover that the moments we had been rushing through were actually the point all along. The poem is not the punctuation at the end; it is the line breaks, the breath, the space between words.

Lingering is not a rejection of action. It is a recognition that action and stillness are not opposites; they are partners in the rhythm of a full life. The musician knows this. The athlete knows this. The farmer knows this. There is a time to plant and a time to let the field lie fallow. Our culture has lost the trust in fallow time, but it is precisely in the fallow periods that the soil regains its richness. Without them, the field eventually yields nothing but dust.

So I am giving myself permission to linger. I am learning to sit with the discomfort of an unfilled hour. I am practicing the art of staying a little longer, looking a little closer, breathing a little slower. It is not always easy. The old guilt rises up, whispering about wasted time. But I am beginning to suspect that the only truly wasted time is the time we spend without noticing that we are alive. The rest—the slow afternoons, the aimless walks, the quiet cups of tea—is not waste at all. It is the very substance of a life, and it is already waiting for us, if we will only stop long enough to let it in.

The rest—the slow afternoons, the aimless walks, the quiet cups of tea—is not waste at all. It is the very substance of a life, and it is already waiting for us, if we will only stop long enough to let it in.
